traveler: Sabbatai Zevi (Shabbetai Tzvi, later Aziz Mehmed Effendi)
title: The Fasts Turned to Feasts: Smyrna, Gaza, the Tower of Strength, and the Turban
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Smyrna, the Hakham Who Says the Name

stops.name: Smyrna, born on the fast of Av
stops.date_confidence: traditional: 9 Av AM 5386 computes to 1 August 1626 Gregorian, but no birth register survives and Encyclopaedia Judaica warns the date may have been fitted to the tradition retrospectively. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives 23 July 1626, which matches neither the Gregorian nor the Julian rendering of 9 Av (Julian would be 21 July); the discrepancy is not a calendar-conversion artifact and is left unresolved.
stops.campa: The son born to Mordecai Zevi in the Jewish quarter of Smyrna arrives, the tradition holds, on the ninth of Av, the fast that mourns both destroyed Temples and on which the Messiah is said to be born. His father is a poultry dealer out of the Morea who has come up as the agent of an English trading house, and Smyrna is coming up with him: a Levantine port filling with European factors and Iberian exiles, where the correspondence of half the Mediterranean is unloaded and read. No birth register survives. Encyclopaedia Judaica warns the date may have been fitted to the tradition afterwards, and the Jewish Encyclopedia gives 23 July.
suggested_refs: A house near the ancient Agora in Izmir, long associated with him, ruinous in 2015 and since restored
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, the yeshiva of Joseph Escapa
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Jewish Encyclopedia names Escapa as his teacher but gives no dates for the schooling; c. 1638-1644 is inferred from the ordination at about eighteen. No building is identified in any source; the pin is the Smyrna Jewish quarter generally.
stops.campa: He is set to the Talmud under Joseph Escapa, one of Smyrna's senior rabbis, and is addressed as hakham by about his eighteenth year. The law he learns is the law as Maimonides codified it and as the later codes arranged it, a system of permitted and forbidden acts fixed down to the smallest gesture of a meal. He learns it well enough to be ordained in it. Nothing in the record of these years marks out the pupil who will one day stand in a prison on the Dardanelles and bless the God who permits the forbidden.
suggested_refs: The rabbinical academy of Joseph Escapa at Smyrna
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, the years of seclusion
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the ascetic period 1642/1648 without fixing a start; the medical reading is modern and retrospective, made from contemporaries' descriptions rather than from any diagnosis made at the time.
stops.campa: He withdraws from the yeshiva into a solitude of his own: fasting, immersion in cold water, nights over the Zohar that Moses de Leon put into circulation under the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and the Lurianic writings reaching Smyrna from Safed. Those around him record two weathers alternating without cause. Months of black withdrawal in which he speaks to no one: his circle calls that the hiding of the face. Months of exalted lucidity in which he does whatever the exaltation dictates: they call that illumination. Modern readers of the reports diagnose manic-depressive illness, a reading made from those descriptions and no examination.
suggested_refs: The Zohar as it circulated in seventeenth-century Smyrna, in the Lurianic reading out of Safed

stops.name: Smyrna, the Name pronounced aloud
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Jewish Encyclopedia, which places the first revelation of the messianic claim at Smyrna in 1648, his twenty-second year; Encyclopaedia Judaica reports the utterance of the divine name without fixing it to a year.
stops.campa: In a season of exaltation he pronounces the four letters of the Name aloud, as it is written and not as it is read, an act the tradition reserves to the high priest in the sanctuary on one day of the year. A man who says the Name in an ordinary room is either what he claims to be or he is the other thing, and nothing about the deed is ambiguous to the rabbis who hear of it. To a small circle he discloses which of the two he takes himself for: he is the redeemer, and the utterance was the proof. The Jewish Encyclopedia puts this at Smyrna in 1648, his twenty-second year. Encyclopaedia Judaica reports the utterance without fixing it to a year.
suggested_refs: The rabbinic prohibition on pronouncing the Tetragrammaton outside the Temple service
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, banished by the rabbinate
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Jewish Encyclopedia gives c. 1651, Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 1651/1654, and no document fixes the year. The pool's sources do not name which rabbis signed the sentence.
stops.campa: The rabbinate of Smyrna puts him and his followers out of the city. No trial is held and no full excommunication is pronounced. What they do is what a household does with something it cannot keep and will not destroy. He leaves the port his father prospered in and enters a wandering that takes up the next decade, Salonika to Constantinople and back again, an ordained hakham with no congregation and a claim he does not stop making. The sources disagree on the year: 1651 in one account, 1654 in another.
suggested_refs: The communal authority of the Ottoman rabbinate and its power of banishment
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Salonika, the wedding to the Torah scroll
stops.date_confidence: tradition: the ceremony is reported by Baruch of Arezzo and later derivative accounts, not by any contemporary document. Encyclopaedia Judaica places it 1654/1658. The name of the rabbi who expelled him is given as Abraham de Boton by one modern summary and by no primary source; the surname collides with Abraham di Boton of the Lehem Mishneh, dead c. 1605, so the name is omitted here.
stops.campa: In Salonika he invites the rabbis and notables to a feast, sets up a bridal canopy, and has a Torah scroll carried in under it as his bride. The kabbalists present know the figure well: the Torah is the bride of Israel, and the union is among the oldest images in their literature. Performed with a real canopy and real witnesses, it stops being a figure. The rabbis of Salonika banish him from the city. The account comes through believers writing after his death, and no contemporary document records the ceremony at all.
suggested_refs: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, the believers' memorial narrative composed c. 1677
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Constantinople, the circle of Abraham ha-Yakini
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Jewish Encyclopedia gives a Constantinople period of 1653-1658, Encyclopaedia Judaica a single stay of about nine months in 1658. Both cannot stand; neither is preferred here. The forged prophecy is attested as text by the Jewish Encyclopedia, which attributes the forgery to ha-Yakini himself.
stops.campa: In Constantinople he falls in with the preacher Abraham ha-Yakini, a man with a fine library and a finer hand. A parchment surfaces in this circle, worn and aged, titled the Great Wisdom of Solomon, opening with a voice heard by Abraham after forty years in a cave and announcing that a son will be born to Mordecai Zevi who will humble the great dragon. It is a forgery, and the Jewish Encyclopedia lays it at ha-Yakini's own door. Sabbatai reads it as confirmation.
stops.quote: A son will be born in the year 5386 [1626] to Mordecai Zebi; and he will be called Shabbethai. He will humble the great dragon; . . . he, the true Messiah, will sit upon My [God's] throne.
stops.quote_source: Hokhmat Shelomo ha-Gedolah, the forged prophecy circulated in Abraham ha-Yakini's circle, quoted in Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)
suggested_refs: The pseudepigraphic Hokhmat Shelomo ha-Gedolah, a seventeenth-century forgery in an antique hand
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, the quiet return
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the Jewish Encyclopedia's sequence places a Smyrna interval between the Constantinople years and the departure east, with no events recorded in it. The dates are the gap between two better-attested periods, not a datum.
stops.campa: He comes back to Smyrna and for three years does nothing that anyone writes down. No pronouncement, no ceremony, no expulsion. The sources move from Constantinople to Cairo and pass through the interval without a sentence, and the believers who later collected every gesture of his life collected nothing out of here. He is in his middle thirties when he leaves. The route runs by Rhodes and Cairo rather than straight, the ordinary Aegean coasting of a man traveling on other men's ships.
suggested_refs: The undocumented Smyrna interval, c. 1659-1662
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Rhodes, the passage south
stops.date_confidence: attested in one clause only: Encyclopaedia Judaica states that in late 1662 he traveled to Jerusalem by way of Rhodes and Cairo. The Jewish Encyclopedia does not mention Rhodes. Nothing about the stay is recorded. The pin is the Jewish quarter around the Kahal Shalom synagogue rather than the harbour.
stops.campa: The ship touches at Rhodes, where a Jewish quarter has stood inside the walls since long before the Ottomans took the island from the knights, and where the road from the Aegean to Alexandria has always broken its journey. He is traveling as a private man and the record treats him as one. Encyclopaedia Judaica gives the whole stop in a single clause: to Jerusalem, by way of Rhodes and Cairo. How long he stayed, whom he saw, whether the quarter had yet heard what happened at Salonika: none of it survives, and the Jewish Encyclopedia does not mention Rhodes at all.
suggested_refs: The Kahal Shalom synagogue and the Juderia of Rhodes old town

stops.name: Cairo, the house of Raphael Joseph
stops.date_confidence: contested: Wikipedia and the Jewish Encyclopedia give a Cairo residence of about 1660-1662; Encyclopaedia Judaica gives a 1663 emissary return running to spring 1665. There may be two stays or one, and the sources do not reconcile. The pin is the canonical Fustat coordinate inherited from the Maimonides file; the seventeenth-century Harat al-Yahud lay somewhat north of it, off Sharia al-Muizz.
stops.campa: In Cairo he is taken into the house of Raphael Joseph Halabi, mint master and tax farmer, the wealthiest Jew in Egypt, whose household works as a standing clearing station for kabbalists, petitioners, and men arriving with revelations. Sabbatai is received there as one of them, and financed. He will come back to this house, and its money will pay for a good deal of what follows. The sources place his Cairo residence variously at 1660 to 1662 and at 1663 to 1665. Whether that is two stays or one, no document decides.
suggested_refs: The household of Raphael Joseph Halabi, patron of the Egyptian kabbalists
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the psalms sung at night
stops.date_confidence: attested as practice, inferred as place: the Jewish Encyclopedia records ascetic practice and night psalm-singing at Jerusalem c. 1663 without naming a site. The pin is the canonical Temple Mount coordinate inherited from the Evliya Celebi file; no source places him specifically at the Western Wall.
stops.campa: He settles in Jerusalem and gives himself to the discipline he taught himself alone in Smyrna: fasting, immersion, and the singing of psalms through the night in the streets below the Temple platform, where the retaining wall of Herod's enclosure is the only masonry of the House still standing. He has a voice, and the voice is what gathers people. Those who follow him here are following a singer and an ascetic. In Jerusalem he makes no announcement about himself at all.
suggested_refs: The Temple platform and its western retaining wall, the site of the messianic restoration his followers later expected
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Jerusalem, sent out as emissary
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia and Encyclopaedia Judaica both record the emissary mission to Egypt on the community's behalf; the month is a reconstruction from the autumn dating in the pool.
stops.campa: The community is being crushed by an Ottoman tax demand it cannot meet, and it needs a man who can ask Raphael Joseph in Cairo for money and be given it. They choose Sabbatai. It is the one office the record shows him holding by ordinary appointment, on ordinary business, trusted with other people's survival. The letters he carries are the ordinary letters of such an errand, and none of them survive. He rides out of Jerusalem an emissary of the Jerusalem poor and comes back, some eighteen months later, something else.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman fiscal burden on the Jerusalem Jewish community in the 1660s

stops.name: Cairo, the marriage to Sarah
stops.date_confidence: conventional: 31 March 1664 is the date given by Encyclopaedia Judaica. The Jewish Encyclopedia places the marriage in Cairo but inside its 1660-1662 window, a disagreement of several years that no source reconciles. The pin is the inherited Fustat coordinate, not a located house.
stops.campa: Sarah arrives in Cairo out of Poland, an orphan of the Cossack violence of 1648, having told whoever would listen that she was destined to marry the Messiah. Sabbatai hears of her and sends for her. In Raphael Joseph's house they are married, a woman who has said she will marry the Messiah and a man who has said he is the Messiah; the household takes the fit between the two claims as evidence of both. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the wedding to the last day of March 1664. The Jewish Encyclopedia puts it years earlier, inside its 1660 to 1662 window, and nothing reconciles the two.
suggested_refs: The 1648 Chmielnicki massacres in Poland, which produced Sarah's orphaning and much of the movement's later audience
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

segments.name: Gaza: the Prophet Finds His Messiah

stops.name: Gaza, seeking a cure from Nathan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the Gaza journey to April 1665 and Wikipedia confirms that Nathan first received him as a physician receives a patient. The day is a reconstruction. Nathan's claim to a February throne-vision survives only in a letter of 1667, two years after the fact.
stops.campa: He goes to Gaza to find a young man named Nathan Benjamin ha-Levi, barely twenty, who has a reputation for reading a soul and prescribing the repentance that will heal it. Sabbatai wants the black weather lifted. He comes as a patient. Nathan examines him and refuses the office of physician outright: there is nothing in this soul to mend, because this is the soul of the Messiah, and he says he has already seen the name Sabbatai Zevi engraved on the throne of glory in a vision the previous February.
stops.quote: When I had attained the age of twenty, I began to study the book Zohar and some of the Lurianic writings... the spirit came over me, my hair stood on end and my knees shook and I beheld the merkabah, and I saw visions of God all day long and all night...
stops.quote_source: Nathan of Gaza, autobiographical letter of 1673 describing his own prophetic formation, quoted in Gershom Scholem, Sabbatai Sevi: The Mystical Messiah (Princeton, 1973), p. 204
suggested_refs: Nathan of Gaza's letter of 1667, the earliest surviving account of the February 1665 throne-vision

stops.name: Gaza, the proclamation of 17 Sivan
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 31 May 1665, the seventeenth of Sivan. The common framing of this as a Shavuot proclamation is wrong by eleven days: 6 Sivan AM 5425 falls on 20 May 1665. Nathan's possession-trance is what happened on Shavuot night; the proclamation is a separate, later event.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of Sivan, before a gathering in Gaza, he says it in public and without hedging. Nathan proclaims him, the circle proclaims him, and messengers go out that same season toward Aleppo, Smyrna, Constantinople, Livorno, and Amsterdam with the news that the redemption has begun and that its completion falls in the coming year. Eleven days earlier, on the night of Shavuot, Nathan had fallen into his trance before witnesses. Most accounts tell the two as one event. They are not one event.
suggested_refs: The Sabbatean circular letters of 1665, the movement's first mass communication

stops.name: Aleppo, the news outrunning the man
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Jewish Encyclopedia records the enthusiastic Aleppo reception en route to Smyrna; the dates 20 July to 12 August come from the pool's chronology and are not fixed by a document seen this session. The pin is the canonical Aleppo citadel coordinate inherited from the Evliya Celebi file.
stops.campa: Coming north from Gaza he is received at Aleppo by merchants and scholars who have already read the letters; the news has outrun him and arrives everywhere ahead of him from here on. Aleppo is where the caravan roads out of Persia meet the routes down to the Mediterranean ports, and where the European factors keep their correspondents, so what is said in its khans reaches Livorno in weeks and Amsterdam within two months. The Jewish Encyclopedia records the reception and attaches no date to it; the July and August days given here come from a chronology this session could not confirm.
suggested_refs: The khans and merchant correspondence networks of Ottoman Aleppo, the movement's first relay toward Europe
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

segments.name: Smyrna, the Year the Fasts Became Feasts

stops.name: Smyrna, the return of the claimant
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the arrival to September 1665, the Jewish Encyclopedia the public declaration to the autumn of that year.
stops.campa: He comes home to the city that expelled him fourteen years earlier and finds it ready for him. Fasts are cancelled by his word and kept as feasts. Prophecy breaks out in the streets, in women and children as much as in men. Merchants stop buying, households sell what they have and wait for the ships that will carry Israel home. The rabbinate that banished him is a minority in its own community now and knows it. He is thirty-nine years old and has not held an office here since he was eighteen.
suggested_refs: The abolition of the fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz and its keeping as a feast in Sabbatean communities
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, the doors of the Portuguese synagogue
stops.date_confidence: attested with a one-day correction: Encyclopaedia Judaica has the crowd storming an opponent's house on Friday 11 December and Sabbatai forcing the locked doors of the Portuguese congregation 'on the following day,' which computes to Saturday 12 December 1665. The synagogue's exact location in the quarter is not identified in any source.
stops.campa: On the Friday a crowd of his followers storms the house of one of his opponents. On the Sabbath day following he comes himself to the Portuguese congregation, whose officers have locked the doors against him, and has them broken open. It is the plainest act of the whole Smyrna year: a door taken off its hinges in front of the congregation, with no argument about communal authority attached to it. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the storming to the eleventh and the doors to the day after, which was a Saturday.
stops.quote: The first-begotten Son of God, Shabbethai Tsebi, Messiah and Redeemer of the people of Israel, to all the sons of Israel, Peace! Since ye have been deemed worthy to behold the great day and the fulfilment of God's word by the Prophets, your lament and sorrow must be changed into joy, and your fasting into merriment; for ye shall weep no more.
stops.quote_source: Circular letter drafted by Samuel Primo and issued in Sabbatai Zevi's name, Smyrna, December 1665, quoted in Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)
suggested_refs: The Portuguese congregation of Smyrna, whose doors were forced in December 1665
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna, the deposition of Aaron Lapapa
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the displacement of Lapapa to 23 December 1665; the Jewish Encyclopedia records the deposition without a day.
stops.campa: Aaron Lapapa holds a chief rabbinical seat of Smyrna and refuses him. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates his displacement to the twenty-third of December, eleven days after the synagogue doors: he is out, deposed by acclamation of a community that no longer requires its rabbinate's agreement about anything. The machinery of an Ottoman Jewish community is not built to be captured; it is built to outlast whoever tries. A man who holds no office in it, and never has, captures it inside a month.
suggested_refs: The rabbinical opposition in Smyrna, of which Aaron Lapapa was the last officeholder to resist
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Smyrna harbour, sailing for the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the departure by sea to 30 December 1665. The harbour pin is the historic Smyrna quay area, approximate rather than a located mole.
stops.campa: He takes ship at the quay a week after the deposition, bound for Constantinople. His followers understand the voyage precisely: he is going to the imperial city to take the crown off the sultan's head without violence, by the word alone, as the prophecies now in circulation say he will. He travels with a small party and no army. In Europe the reports of this sailing arrive as reports of a fleet. What leaves Smyrna at the end of December is a chartered ship in winter weather.
stops.quote: All the world here is talking of a rumour of the return of the Israelites ... to their own country. ... Should the news be confirmed, it may bring about a revolution in all things.
stops.quote_source: Henry Oldenburg to Baruch Spinoza, 8 December 1665, as quoted in Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906); the correspondence itself could not be reached directly this session
suggested_refs: Henry Oldenburg's letter to Spinoza of 8 December 1665, reporting the rumour in London and Amsterdam

stops.name: Sea of Marmara, taken at sea
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by Encyclopaedia Judaica; the coordinate is an approximate point in the Marmara, since no source gives the position of the interception.
stops.campa: Winter weather holds the crossing for weeks, and the delay is enough. The grand vizier's officers come out to the ship in the Marmara and take him at sea, in the water between the Aegean and the capital, before anyone in Constantinople has laid eyes on him. It is the first move the Ottoman state makes in the affair, and it is made quietly, by boat, with no proclamation and no troops behind it. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the interception to the sixth of February 1666 and gives no position for it; the pin here is a guess at open water.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman interception of 6 February 1666 in the Sea of Marmara
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Constantinople, in chains before the vizier's officers
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 8 February 1666 for the landing in chains. Wikipedia names the grand vizier Koprulzade Fazil Ahmed Pasha as the authority ordering the imprisonment. The Imperial Council chamber has no separate coordinate; the pin is the old city generally.
stops.campa: He is brought ashore in chains and put before the officers of the grand vizier, Koprulzade Fazil Ahmed Pasha. Asked what he claims, he denies political pretension of any kind. He is neither tortured nor executed; the empire, which has hanged men for less noise than his followers have been making in Smyrna, files him as a disturbance and sends him to prison. No Ottoman record of the session survives. What is known of what he said in that room reaches us through Encyclopaedia Judaica and the Jewish Encyclopedia.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman Imperial Council under Koprulzade Fazil Ahmed Pasha, February 1666

stops.name: Gallipoli, the Tower of Strength
stops.date_confidence: attested as event, unresolved as site: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the transfer to 19 April 1666 and names the fortress of Gallipoli; the Jewish Encyclopedia calls the prison Abydos without locating it. The pin follows Encyclopaedia Judaica and sits at Gelibolu. The identification with Kilitbahir Castle, made in some summaries, is unsupported: Kilitbahir is thirty-five kilometres south on the European bank, and ancient Abydos was on the Asian side near Nara Burnu.
stops.campa: He is moved out of the capital to the fortress on the strait, and the imprisonment turns at once into something the Ottomans did not intend. His followers rename the fortress Migdal Oz, the Tower of Strength, and come to it from Poland, from Italy, from Egypt, paying the guards for admission the way pilgrims pay at a shrine. He holds court in a cell. Money arrives with the pilgrims, and the guards, who are being paid better than the sultan pays them, let it go on arriving.
suggested_refs: The fortress the believers called Migdal Oz, whose location on the strait is not settled between Gelibolu and the Abydos bank
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Gallipoli, the paschal lamb and the forbidden fat
stops.date_confidence: attested as act, reconstructed as date: Wikipedia records that he violated halakhah by slaughtering a paschal lamb on arrival at the fortress; Passover 5426 fell immediately after the 19 April transfer, and 20 April is the reconstruction. The wording of the blessing is reported in the pool's sources and not traced to a manuscript this session.
stops.campa: At Passover in the fortress he has a lamb slaughtered and roasted whole, and eats it with its fat, which the law forbids absolutely and which no reading softens. The thing is done formally, aloud, in front of witnesses who will report it, and it announces that in the age now beginning the categories of permitted and forbidden have changed hands into his. Wikipedia records the act; the wording of the blessing he composed for it comes through the literature and has not been traced to any manuscript. What he said over the lamb was: blessed are You, who permits the forbidden.
suggested_refs: The antinomian blessing 'who permits the forbidden,' the doctrinal core of the strange acts

stops.name: Gallipoli, the dispute with Nehemiah ha-Kohen
stops.date_confidence: attested as dispute, contested as cause: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates Nehemiah ha-Kohen's arrival to 3 or 4 September 1666 and Wikipedia confirms that the Polish communities sent him and that he declared Sabbatai an impostor. Whether he then denounced him to the Ottoman authorities, and whether that denunciation produced the summons to Adrianople, is not established by any source.
stops.campa: The Polish communities send Nehemiah ha-Kohen, a kabbalist of their own, to examine him, and the two dispute at the fortress for three days over the doctrine of the Messiah. Nehemiah leaves declaring him an impostor. What he did after that is reported three different ways: that he converted to Islam, that he feigned conversion to get a hearing, that he went to the authorities and denounced Sabbatai as a rebel. The dispute is attested. The causal link to the summons that follows within days is not.
suggested_refs: The Polish rabbinical delegation of 1666 and Nehemiah ha-Kohen's report

stops.name: Adrianople, before the sultan's court
stops.date_confidence: attested as summons, unverified as scene: Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia place him before Mehmed IV's court at Adrianople on 15 September 1666. The archery ordeal is reported by Paul Rycaut, English consul at Smyrna, in his History of the Turkish Empire of 1680; no Ottoman transcript of the session survives to confirm or refute it.
stops.campa: He is brought up to Adrianople, where Mehmed IV keeps his court and his hunting, and set before the divan with the sultan said to be watching from behind a lattice. The account that reaches Europe, through the English consul Paul Rycaut, has the court offer him a choice: strip and stand for the archers, and if the arrows will not pierce him the claim is proved, or else take the turban. No Ottoman record of the session survives. Rycaut published fourteen years later and was not in the room.
suggested_refs: Paul Rycaut, The History of the Turkish Empire (London, 1680), the source of the archery story
sources: Paul Rycaut, The History of the Turkish Empire (1680)

stops.name: Adrianople, the turban taken
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Jewish Encyclopedia and Wikipedia both give 16 September 1666, which computes to 16 Elul AM 5426, the date Scholem gives. Encyclopaedia Judaica's 15 September is reconciled by the Jewish Encyclopedia's phrasing, that he was brought before the sultan on the fifteenth and converted 'on the following day.' The stipend is given by Encyclopaedia Judaica as 150 piasters a day; the akce figure repeated elsewhere is a silent and large conversion, and the unit is disputed.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of September he puts on the turban. He is given the name Mehmed, the honorific effendi, the palace rank of keeper of the gates, and a daily state stipend that Encyclopaedia Judaica records as 150 piasters. In Poland, in Italy, in Amsterdam and Hamburg, communities that have sold their houses and fixed the date of departure hear of it over the following weeks. Some burn the letters. Nathan of Gaza, who is not there, begins at once to explain that the apostasy is the deepest act of the redemption and had to happen.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman court rank of kapici bashi and the pension granted to the convert Mehmed Effendi
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Adrianople, the letter to his brother Elijah
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the letter is quoted in the Jewish Encyclopedia by way of Wikipedia and dates itself to the ninth day of his regeneration, which places it around 24 September 1666. The manuscript itself was not reached this session, and the wording stands one remove from the cited primary.
stops.campa: Nine days after the turban he writes to his brother Elijah in Smyrna. The letter does not apologise and does not explain. What happened was done to him by God, in the grammar of the creation account: He commanded, and it was so. He dates it from the ninth day of his regeneration, counting a new life from the conversion the way a convert counts. Whether he believed that, or was writing what a man newly on a state pension has to write, the letter does not say, and nothing else that survives says either.
stops.quote: God has made me an Ishmaelite; He commanded, and it was done. The ninth day of my regeneration.
stops.quote_source: Sabbatai Zevi to his brother Elijah, Adrianople, c. late September 1666, quoted in Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)
suggested_refs: The conversion letters of autumn 1666, the founding texts of Sabbatean apologetics
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Adrianople, Sarah under the turban
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia states only that Sarah and about three hundred families of followers also converted, with no date; Encyclopaedia Judaica gives no timing either. The commonly repeated 'about a week after' is unsupported, and the Muslim name Fatima comes from the pool alone and is not corroborated in any source reached this session.
stops.campa: Sarah converts too. With her go something like three hundred families of believers, who take the turban in the same season and do not stop being what they were. The reports give her a Muslim name and disagree about it. They give no date, no scene, and no sentence of hers about any of it, though she had told half the Mediterranean she would marry the Messiah and the record kept that one. Wikipedia has the whole of her conversion in a single clause: Sarah and approximately three hundred families among his followers also converted to Islam.
suggested_refs: The mass conversion of roughly three hundred believer families in 1666, the seed of the Donme

stops.name: Adrianople, the two religions kept at once
stops.date_confidence: attested as period, synthesised as description: Encyclopaedia Judaica records that from 1667 to 1672 he lived at Adrianople and Constantinople outwardly practising Islam while privately continuing Jewish rites and teaching disciples. The specific texture comes from the believer narrative of Baruch of Arezzo, a partisan witness writing after the death.
stops.campa: For six years he lives in Adrianople as Mehmed Effendi, drawing the stipend, going to the mosque, and receiving Jewish disciples in his house, where the festivals are kept in altered form and the prayers are said in Hebrew. The Ottoman authorities know, and for six years they do not much mind; a convert with odd habits is not a matter of state. Baruch of Arezzo, writing afterwards from inside the faith, records the mosque attendance with no embarrassment at all, as part of the work.
stops.quote: Nearly every day he would go to the mosque, their prayer-house, where he would pray before the Lord his God and perform great acts of mending.
stops.quote_source: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. David J. Halperin, in Sabbatai Zevi: Testimonies to a Fallen Messiah (2007), excerpted at posenlibrary.com
suggested_refs: Baruch of Arezzo's Zikaron li-vene Yisrael and the Najara Chronicle, the two believer accounts of the double observance
sources: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. Halperin (2007), via posenlibrary.com

stops.name: Adrianople, the letter signed in two languages
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, approximate as date: the letter is preserved in Baruch of Arezzo's Zikaron li-vene Yisrael and dated by Halperin's edition only to c. 1671-1673, within the Adrianople residence. The month and day here are an ordering device with no evidential value.
stops.campa: Two rabbis are accused before him of doubting his faith, and he answers them by letter. He does not threaten and he does not curse. He quotes Proverbs at them, one rebuke landing harder on a man of understanding than a hundred beatings on a fool, and tells them to be valiant instead in the truth of the God of Truth. Then he signs it: your brother Me'emet, which is the Turkish name he took and the Hebrew word for truth at the same time, and under that, this is the gate of the Lord, Zevi. Halperin's edition can date the letter no closer than somewhere in the Adrianople years.
stops.quote: Thus speaks your brother Me'emet, the faith of the Lord God of Truth. This is the gate of the Lord, Zevi.
stops.quote_source: Sabbatai Zevi, letter to two rabbis, preserved in Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. David J. Halperin, in Sabbatai Zevi: Testimonies to a Fallen Messiah (2007), pp. 75-78, excerpted at posenlibrary.com
suggested_refs: The letters of Sabbatai Zevi preserved inside Baruch of Arezzo's believer narrative
sources: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. Halperin (2007), via posenlibrary.com

stops.name: Adrianople, the circumcision of Ishmael Mordecai
stops.date_confidence: reported by believers, not independently attested: the scene comes from Baruch of Arezzo, whose translated text was read directly, and from the Najara Chronicle as cited in the pool; neither Wikipedia nor the Jewish Encyclopedia corroborates it. The year 1671 follows the pool's dating of Solomon Najara's eyewitness record and is not fixed by a document.
stops.campa: A son is born to him and Sarah after the conversion, and on the eighth day he circumcises the boy himself, aloud, with wine and the blessings said at full voice, in the open, with Turks watching. He gives the child the name Ishmael Mordecai: the name of Abraham's other son, the one sent out into the desert who became a nation, joined to the name of his own father. Solomon Najara, living in the household, writes the scene down, and so does Baruch of Arezzo, neither of them treating it as a contradiction of anything. No source outside the believers mentions the boy at all.
stops.quote: After he had put the pure turban on his head, he made love to his Ashkenazi wife. She conceived; she bore him a son. On the eighth day he circumcised the infant with his own hands, with wine and blessings recited in a loud voice. He did this in full view of the Turks. He gave the baby the name "Ishmael Mordecai."
stops.quote_source: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. David J. Halperin, in Sabbatai Zevi: Testimonies to a Fallen Messiah (2007), excerpted at posenlibrary.com
suggested_refs: The Najara Chronicle, kept by a believer resident in the Adrianople household
sources: Baruch of Arezzo, Zikaron li-vene Yisrael, trans. Halperin (2007), via posenlibrary.com

stops.name: Adrianople, Sarah divorced and taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested by Encyclopaedia Judaica, which dates the divorce and reconciliation to April 1671 and reports Nathan of Gaza's correspondence as corroboration; no source reached this session gives the grounds, the duration, or anything of Sarah's own account.
stops.campa: In April he divorces Sarah, and takes her back inside the same season. The believers around him record the episode without explanation, as they record the other exaltations, and Nathan of Gaza's correspondence refers to it. She has been at his side since the house in Cairo, has taken the turban when he took it, and was a figure in the movement in her own right, the woman who said before any of it happened that she would marry the Messiah. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates both the divorce and the reconciliation to April 1671 and gives no grounds for either.
suggested_refs: Nathan of Gaza's correspondence of the Adrianople years, partisan and internal

stops.name: Constantinople, the petition against the Jews
stops.date_confidence: single partisan witness: the episode rests entirely on a disapproving report by Nathan of Gaza, as relayed in the pool, and was not corroborated by any source reached this session. Treated as tradition, not as attested fact.
stops.campa: He asks the sultan for authority over the Jews of Constantinople who have rejected him, and specifically for the power to punish them. The sultan does not answer. Here the claim to be Messiah becomes a request for police power over other Jews, once, and nowhere else in the life. The whole episode rests on Nathan of Gaza, by now his prophet and his critic at the same time, who writes about it with disgust and would have no reason to invent a story that damages his own case. No other source mentions it.
suggested_refs: Nathan of Gaza's critical reports of the post-conversion years

stops.name: Constantinople, the second arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica gives August 1672 and locates the arrest at Constantinople. One geographical summary in the pool places it at Adrianople, contradicting its own supporting quotation, which is headed Constantinople; the Constantinople reading is followed here.
stops.campa: After six years the tolerance runs out. He is arrested at Constantinople in August 1672 on complaints that he keeps two religions at once, that Hebrew singing goes on in his house at night, and that money moves through his circle in ways the authorities dislike. None of the charges is theological; the empire has no objection to a bad Muslim, and every objection to a convert running a congregation. One summary in circulation puts the arrest at Adrianople while quoting a passage headed Constantinople. Encyclopaedia Judaica is followed here.
suggested_refs: The Ottoman proceedings of August 1672 against the convert Mehmed Effendi
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Ulcinj, exile to the edge of the empire
stops.date_confidence: attested: Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the exile order to January 1673 and Wikipedia confirms Ulcinj as the place from 1673. The 1673 letter quoted here was read in a secondary article that reproduces it; the underlying manuscript was not traced, so the translated wording carries some risk.
stops.campa: The order of January 1673 sends him to Dulcigno, a walled Adriatic town on the far edge of the empire, weeks of travel from any Jewish community of size. His followers call the place Alkum. The stipend follows him, and so do Sarah, a small household, and letters in both directions, more of them than the isolation ought to allow. From here he instructs the believers to chop the faith back to the root and bury the root in their hearts, keeping nothing of it visible. The letter carrying that instruction was read in an article reproducing it; the manuscript behind it was not traced.
stops.quote: Chop off utterly the branches of that faith till nothing remains buried in your hearts but the root alone... Bury this my very great faith.
stops.quote_source: Letter of Sabbatai Zevi, 1673, written from Ottoman Albania, quoted in 'In Search of Sabbatai Zevi,' k-larevue.com (2021)
suggested_refs: The doctrine of concealment as transmitted to the believers from Alkum

stops.name: Ulcinj, the death of Sarah
stops.date_confidence: attested as year, contested as place: Wikipedia states that his wife died at Ulcinj in 1674; Encyclopaedia Judaica gives the year with no place, and one summary in the pool infers Adrianople, a town they had both left the year before. Ulcinj is followed here. No month, no burial site, and no cause is recorded anywhere.
stops.campa: Sarah dies at Ulcinj. She has been with him ten years, from the house in Cairo through Gaza, Smyrna, the fortress on the strait, the turban, and the exile, converting when he converted, divorced in April and married again by summer. No account records where she is buried, or of what she died, or how old she was. One summary places her death at Adrianople, which she had left with him the year before. What the record keeps of the end of her life is a year.
suggested_refs: The absent record of Sarah's death and burial at Ulcinj

stops.name: Ulcinj, the marriage to Esther
stops.date_confidence: reported, not documented: Encyclopaedia Judaica gives the second marriage as 1674/1675 to Esther, also called Jochebed, Muslim name reported as Ayse, daughter of the convert Joseph Philosophos. The Jewish rite of the ceremony comes from the pool alone and was not corroborated in any source reached this session.
stops.campa: He marries again, a daughter of Joseph Filosof, a Salonika rabbi who has followed him into Islam. She is called Esther among the believers, Jochebed in some accounts, and Ayse under the turban, and she carries three names for the same reason that he carries two. Encyclopaedia Judaica dates the marriage to 1674 or 1675 and does not choose between them. That the ceremony was performed by Jewish rite, by a man nine years a Muslim, in an Ottoman town where nobody is watching closely, is reported with no source behind it.
suggested_refs: The family of Joseph Filosof of Salonika, converts who became the nucleus of the Donme

stops.name: Ulcinj, the letter to Berat asking for a mahzor
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance, uncorroborated in detail: Wikipedia confirms that in August 1676 he wrote to Berat requesting religious books. The identification of the letter with Ben-Zvi Institute MS 2262, fol. 79, and the signature from Alkum, come from the pool and manuscript-catalogue descriptions not independently reached this session.
stops.campa: A month before he dies he writes to the Jews of Berat, up the Albanian coast, asking them urgently to send him a mahzor, the prayer book for the Days of Awe. He is Mehmed Effendi, pensioner of the sultan, ten years under the turban, and what he wants before the New Year is the Hebrew liturgy of repentance in a book he can hold. The letter survives in his own hand, signed from Alkum, and it asks twice. Nobody has recorded whether the book reached him before the fast, or at all.
suggested_refs: Ben-Zvi Institute MS 2262, fol. 79: the last surviving autograph letter, signed at Alkum

stops.name: Ulcinj, the visit of Cardozo
stops.date_confidence: tradition drawn from an interested witness: Encyclopaedia Judaica reports the visit on the strength of Abraham Miguel Cardozo's own later autobiographical writings, which are self-justifying. No independent confirmation was found this session.
stops.campa: Abraham Miguel Cardozo, who has built an entire theology on the apostasy of a man he has never met, arrives at Ulcinj with Joseph Carrillo twelve days before the end. What passed between them is known only from what Cardozo wrote afterwards, and Cardozo wrote a great deal afterwards, in his own interest. He came a long way to a small Adriatic town to find out whether the doctrine held up with the man standing in front of him. He does not say clearly.
suggested_refs: Abraham Miguel Cardozo's autobiographical writings, the sole witness to the Ulcinj visit

stops.name: Ulcinj, death on the Day of Atonement
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia gives c. 17 September 1676, which computes to 10 Tishri AM 5437, Yom Kippur. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives 30 September, hedged with 'according to some'; that figure matches neither the Gregorian nor the Julian rendering of Yom Kippur 5437 and is a straightforward source disagreement, not a calendar artifact.
stops.campa: He dies at Ulcinj on the Day of Atonement, fifty years old, in a town where hardly anyone would have known what day it was. No account gives an execution, a poisoning, or any violence: an ordinary death, on the fast that mourns and asks forgiveness, in the fiftieth year of a life that began, by tradition, on the fast that mourns the Temple. Nathan of Gaza, who outlives him by four years, announces that he has not died at all but has been absorbed into the supernal lights and will return.
suggested_refs: Nathan of Gaza's doctrine of the occultation, which kept the movement alive past the death
sources: Kohler and Malter, 'Shabbethai Zebi b. Mordecai,' Jewish Encyclopedia (1901-1906)

stops.name: Ulcinj, the turbe of Murat Dadaj
stops.date_confidence: local tradition only: the identification of the Murat Dadaj turbe as his grave rests on Ulcinj and Sabbatean tradition as relayed in the pool; the Wikipedia articles on Ulcinj and Ulcinj Old Town do not mention his burial. No inscription and no excavation supports it. The date is the day after the death and orders the stop; it is not a recorded burial date.
stops.campa: Where they put him is not recorded by anyone who was there. Local tradition in Ulcinj points to a small domed Islamic tomb, the turbe called Murat Dadaj, and says that is the grave. No inscription supports it and no excavation has tested it. Donme pilgrims came from Salonika to a tomb of his into the early twentieth century, which means that a grave was being pointed out to them, somewhere, by somebody. Research published in 1985 argued for Dulcigno against the rival Albanian claim.
suggested_refs: The Murat Dadaj turbe at Ulcinj; a statue of Sabbatai Zevi is reported standing in the town, on weak evidence

stops.name: Berat, the rival tomb in the mosque yard
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition: Wikipedia states that his tomb was believed to lie at a Sufi lodge built in the yard of the King's Mosque at Berat, and that it stood until 1967. The date here is an ordering device with no evidential value. That 1967 is the year of Albania's nationwide closure of religious buildings is inference, not a statement of the source.
stops.campa: The rival claim is at Berat, where a Sufi lodge stood in the courtyard of the King's Mosque and was said to hold him. The tomb was there long enough for pilgrims to visit and for the identification to pass into local knowledge, and it stood until 1967, when Albania shut and pulled down its religious buildings wholesale. The claim has one plain fact working against it, which is the letter. A man living at Berat does not write to Berat asking Berat to send him a prayer book.
suggested_refs: The tekke in the yard of the Xhamia e Mbretit at Berat, demolished 1967

stops.name: Salonika, the household that stayed
stops.date_confidence: attested as event, contested as leadership: Wikipedia's Donmeh article dates the mass adhesion to 1683, shortly after Nathan of Gaza's death, with about three thousand Sabbateans converting, and credits Joseph Filosof, Esther's father, with a key role in founding the sect. The common attribution of the 1683 adhesion to Jacob Querido is not supported there; Querido appears as Esther's brother and founder of the later breakaway Jacobite faction.
stops.campa: His widow, his brother, and his children go from Ulcinj to Salonika after the death, to her father's house. Seven years later, in the year Nathan of Gaza dies, some three thousand Sabbateans in Salonika put on the turban together and keep the Jewish observance behind it. They are called the Donme, the turned. Joseph Filosof's circle stands at the centre of the adhesion; Jacob Querido, Esther's brother, breaks away later claiming to be Sabbatai himself come back. The mosque their descendants build in the city is still standing.
suggested_refs: The Yeni Mosque of Thessaloniki, built c. 1902 by the Donme community and used until 1923
The Sazanikos of Edirne, the earliest organised post-conversion believer community
